title: نجم إشبيلية السابق يفجرالريال: ألا يخجل من شكواه ضد الحكام؟.. أي كرة قدم هذه؟!
summary: القرارات التحكيمية تسيل الحبر
body: القرارات التحكيمية تسيل الحبر صعّد أنتونيتو، لاعب إشبيلية السابق، انتقاداته للتحكيم عقب خسارة الفريق الأندلسي أمام ريال مدريد بنتيجة (4-1) على ملعب سانتياجو برنابيو، معترضًا على عدم مراجعة لقطة تدخل أردا جولر على بيكي فيرنانديز، إلى جانب قرارات أخرى رأى أنها أثرت في مجريات اللقاء. وقال أنتونيتو، في تصريحات عبر إذاعة إشبيلية الرسمية: "ألا يخجل ريال مدريد من التذمر من الحكام؟ عذرهم أنهم لم يروا ضربة الكوع التي تعرض لها بيكي بوضوح، رغم أن النتيجة كانت 0-0، كما تعلمون. إنها لقطة حاسمة يدّعون أنهم لم يروها. أي نوع من كرة القدم هذه؟ ألا تخجل رابطة الدوري الإسباني وتقنية حكم الفيديو المساعد؟". وأضاف لاعب إشبيلية السابق أن فريقه تعرض للظلم مجددًا، بحسب وصفه، قائلًا: "كانت هناك هجمة كان يجب أن يُطرد فيها جولر، كما أن الهدف الثاني سبقه خطأ، وكان من المفترض أن يُحتسب لنا هدف أيضًا". وتابع بنبرة غاضبة: "هل يريدون تجهيز الأمور للكلاسيكو ومنع ريال مدريد من التقدم؟ هذا مستحيل. الهدف الوحيد الصحيح في منتصف الملعب كان لريال مدريد. وركلة الجزاء التي احتُسبت كانت سخيفة؛ فهم لا يحتسبون مثل هذه الركلات إلا لريال مدريد وبرشلونة". واختتم أنتونيتو، انتقاداته بالإشارة إلى أن أفضل ما في المباراة، من وجهة نظره، كان انتهاؤها دون إصابات أو بطاقات حمراء، قبل أن يصف ما حدث بأنه "أمر مشين".

title: "كنا نعرف كيف تسير الأمور بالبرنابيو".. لاعبو إشبيلية يفتحون النار على تحكيم مباراة الريال
summary: جدل تحكيمي مستمر
body: جدل تحكيمي مستمر أبدى لاعبو إشبيلية استياءهم من القرارات التحكيمية خلال مواجهة ريال مدريد على ملعب سانتياجو برنابيو، معتبرين أن بعض اللقطات المؤثرة لم تُحتسب لصالحهم، في مباراة شهدت جدلًا بشأن تدخلات على بيكي فيرنانديز، وروبي أوري. وقال خوان إجليسياس، لاعب إشبيلية، في تصريحات لقناة "موفيستار": "كنا داخل المباراة وبذلنا قصارى جهدنا. رأيت مخالفة ضد بيكي، وبدا لي أن الأمر ينطوي على اعتداء، كما أن هناك مخالفة ضد روبي أوري قبل أحد أهداف ريال مدريد، لكن اللقطة لم تُعرض حتى على شاشة التلفزيون". وأضاف: "كنا نعرف ما نحن مقبلون عليه، لكن كانت هناك قرارات خارجة عن إرادتنا. في كثير من الأحيان، لا يمكنك التحدث مع الحكام؛ فهم لا يسمحون بذلك. الأمر ببساطة هو( اخرج.. سأمنحك بطاقة)، وهذا دائمًا الحل الأسهل. كنا نعرف كيف ستسير الأمور هنا". من جانبه، طالب كيكي سالاس، قائد إشبيلية، باحترام فريقه، مؤكدًا أن بعض اللقطات كانت تستحق مراجعة أكثر دقة، وقال: "كانت مخالفة أردا جولر واضحة، ويمكنك رؤية ضربة الكوع التي تعرض لها بيكي. من الواضح أن ذلك رجّح كفة المباراة لصالحهم، ثم أصبحت النتيجة 1-0". وتابع: "لا أفهم لماذا لم يراجعوا تلك اللقطة عبر تقنية حكم الفيديو المساعد. كل ما نطلبه هو الاحترام واحتساب ما حدث. نحن نشعر بالألم، لكن يمكنك أيضًا رؤية مخالفة ضد روبي أوري".

title: حلل هدف وركلة جزاء مبابي.. خبير تحكيمي يصرخ: هل هذا ما ستعرضونه بنهائي مونديال 2030؟
summary: هل استحق إندريك ركلة جزاء؟
body: هل استحق إندريك ركلة جزاء؟ أدلى خبير تحكيمي إسباني، برأيه حول بعض حالات مباراة ريال مدريد وإشبيلية التي جرت اليوم الأحد، ضمن الدوري الإسباني. وشهدت المباراة جدلا تحكيميا كبيرا، لكن كانت هناك مشكلة واضحة للجميع وهي سوء جودة النقل التلفزيوني، وعدم وجود إعادات واضحة لبعض الوقائع الجدلية. واشتكى إيتورالدي جونزاليس، الخبير التحكيمي لصحيفة " آس " وإذاعة "كادينا سير" من عدم وجود لقطات واضحة في واقعة مطالبة لاعبي إشبيلية بطرد أردا جولر في الدقيقة 22. وقال: "أراه يمد ذراعه، لكن لا يمكنك رؤية اصطدامها بوجهه لأن الصور رديئة للغاية. إنه لأمر مؤسف: إذا كنا أفضل دوري في العالم، فلا ينبغي أن يكون مستوى جودة الإعادة بهذا الشكل". وتكرر الأمر في حالات أخرى، فقبل هدف مبابي في الدقيقة 37، والذي كان الثاني لريال مدريد، ادعى إشبيلية وجود خطأ من كوناتي على روبي أوري في بداية الهجمة. ومرة ​​أخرى، لم تكن هناك إعادة واضحة، وهو ما اشتكى منه إيتورالدي قائلاً: "إنه خطأ في وسط الملعب. لو كان خطأً، لكانت بطاقة حمراء، لأن أوري كان منفردًا بالمرمى". وواصل غاضبا: "لكن لا يمكن أن يتكرر هذا، لقطات بهذا السوء في ملعب من فئة الخمس نجوم مزود بـ 32 كاميرا. هذا لا يليق بأفضل دوري في العالم". وتساءل: "هل هذه هي الصور التي سيعرضونها في نهائي كأس العالم الذي نريده في عام 2030؟" وتتنافس إسبانيا مع المغرب على استضافة نهائي بط…

summary: تغلب ليون، على ضيفه نيس، بنتيجة 2-1 مساء الأحد، في ختام الجولة السابعة من عمر الدوري الفرنسي.

body: Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for developing glaucoma or cataracts — but as scientists look more closely at what happens to the eyes over a lifetime, they are finding that people's exposure to air pollution also plays a role in whether they develop these eye conditions. Glaucoma, which affects about 80 million people worldwide , is a group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can lead to permanent vision loss, usually affecting peripheral vision at first and later central vision. Cataracts are even more common, affecting more than 94 million people globally ; the condition occurs when the eye's lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision and, eventually, blindness. Aging raises the risk of both diseases, as do certain medical conditions, such as diabetes. But now, a review of 41 studies suggests that people who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution may also face a greater risk of these diseases. summary: Researchers have found that during the Black Death, when a third of the population of Europe was wiped out, biodiversity fell. Understanding their farming practices could help us increase diversity in modern agriculture.
body: When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes. The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317. This was followed by the Black Death , an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century . body: Sometimes, it takes a great struggle to build towering peaks. And what more thunderous event is there than the clashing of continental plates? Geological pileups have birthed some of the largest and tallest mountains on the planet, including Mount Everest and its Himalayan neighbors. But has there ever been a peak taller than Mount Everest, which stands 29,032 feet (8,849 meters) above sea level? The answer is still a mystery, but there are some geological clues about where the tallest peaks would have been in the ancient past, experts told Live Science. Earth's lost mountains Geologists don't have the level of detail required to pinpoint an exact highest peak hundreds of millions of years ago. "We're never going to get that granularity, unfortunately," Alan Collins , a professor of geology at Adelaide University in Australia, told Live Science. However, clues in residual sediments lodged inside Earth's crust hint at the lost grandeur of primordial snowcaps and summits. Scientists study these crusts to understand how deep they went, which can reveal how tall ancient mountains might have been. title: Physicists froze a 'necklace' of atoms — and witnessed a quantum phenomenon predicted 100 years ago
summary: Atoms confined to a single line can bind into clusters called Bethe strings. A new experiment points to a mix of many such clusters, though the evidence is still indirect.
body: "Necklaces" of ultracold atoms have provided new evidence to support a nearly 100-year-old quantum theory. In 1931, physicists were trying to use quantum mechanics to explain why some materials are magnetic. Then, a young physicist named Hans Bethe looked at a single row of electrons. Each electron's spin can point up or down. Bethe worked out the math for how such a row behaves and found that if a few spins in the row flip, they can stick together and travel down the row as a single unit. Decades later, physicists found that Bethe's method also works for larger particles moving along a line , such as atoms. If those particles attract each other, the math predicts they will bind into clusters called Bethe strings. Now, physicists have found evidence of these clusters in a line of ultracold atoms. The findings were published Aug. 29 in the journal Nature Communications . The discovery may not create new gadgets, but it addresses a fundamental mystery in physics. Everything around us, from magnets to phone chips, consists of countless interacting particles. This makes their behavior difficult to predict. In the new study, scientists fitted an anti-worm drug with nanotech armor, and it directly targeted these painful lesions in laboratory mice. title: One of America's biggest meteor craters is 100 million years younger than we thought — and coincided with a global extinction event
summary: Analysis of tiny zircon crystals buried within the 10-mile-wide Ames crater in northwest Oklahoma suggests that the submerged structure dates back to 370 million years ago, during the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event.
body: One of America's largest meteor craters is around 100 million years younger than scientists thought, which means the ancient impact coincided with — and potentially contributed to — one of the biggest global extinction events in Earth's history, according to a new study. The underground impact structure, known as Ames crater, is located in northern Oklahoma and is named after a small town that sits above the submerged crater. At around 10 miles (16 kilometers) wide, it is the fourth-largest impact structure in the U.S. Ames crater was created when an Eiffel Tower-size space rock slammed into our planet at more than 70,000 mph (110,000 km/h). At the time, the region was covered in a shallow ocean, and the crater was subsequently buried beneath layers of seafloor sediment. Therefore, there are no visible signs of the crater at the surface today. It was only discovered in 1991, when oil prospectors accidentally drilled into it. Until now, researchers thought Ames crater dated to the Ordovician meteor event around 467 million years ago. body: Since June, more than 300 southern right whale ( Eubalaena australis ) calves have died in Argentine Patagonia, in what scientists describe as an "exceptional" die-off. The preliminary figure already far exceeds the previous annual record set in 2012, when 113 southern right whale calves died — the highest number ever documented for the species , both locally and globally. Now, scientists are racing to figure out exactly what's causing the record-breaking die-off. Laboratory analyses of specimens that died this year tested positive for the pathogenic bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae , environmental authorities in Chubut province told Live Science. title: 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds people who died of 'sharp force' injuries, possibly from a Viking raid
summary: A 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds the remains of a father, son and four others ‪who may have been victims of a Viking raid.
body: Six people buried in a single grave in Latvia more than 1,000 years ago may have been killed in a bloody Viking raid, a new study suggests. Genetic research into the deceased — four men, a boy and a girl — reveals family connections: The boy was the son of one of the men, while another man was a third-degree relative, perhaps a first cousin or great uncle, the researchers found. The father, the relative, and one other man died from "sharp force" injuries — maybe wounds from an ax or a sword; but it's unknown how the other three individuals died, the researchers reported in the study, which was published in the September issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports . One possibility is that those in the grave were killed in a battle, maybe with a neighboring community. But suspicion also falls on the Vikings: "We will never know if they were killed in a raid, but it remains a possibility because of the date of the grave" and the fatal trauma suffered by three of the men, said study co-author Elīna Pētersone-Gordina , an archaeologist at the University of Latvia. body: When Christopher Columbus made landfall in the Americas on Oct. 12, 1492, he encountered Indigenous Lucayans living on the Bahamian island now called San Salvador. Columbus wrote in his diary about " great multitudes of men " who greeted him that day, bartered with him and told him about other groups who lived on nearby islands. But within a few decades after Columbus' arrival, the Indigenous people of the Americas were decimated by what anthropologist Eric Wolf called the " Great Dying " — a combination of epidemic disease, warfare and enslavement that led to a rapid decline in the Native population. For centuries, researchers have been trying to figure out how many Indigenous people lived in the Americas just prior to the fateful arrival of European colonizers. The answer to that question has been surprisingly elusive, and estimates based on historical censuses, archaeological sites and land carrying capacity in the Western Hemisphere have varied wildly. title: How did Roman aqueducts get water to go uphill?
summary: Roman aqueducts used gravity to transport water. So how did they get it to go uphill?
body: Aqueducts are some of the ancient Romans' most prominent surviving archaeological remains. These aqueducts relied on gravity to bring down the water to cities gradually. But some, such as the aqueduct at Aspendos in Turkey, had sections where they had to go uphill. So how did the Romans get water to flow upward ? The Romans used a few methods, including siphons and various water-lifting devices, experts told Live Science. Roman aqueduct with inverted siphons that scholars have reconstructed with a virtual modeling simulation. To get water through a valley, the Romans built a "header tank" on one end of the valley and a slightly lower "receiving tank" (or "outlet tank") on the other side. In the valley, they constructed two towers between the tanks, Paul Kessener , a researcher in the Department of Language and Culture Studies at Radboud University in the Netherlands, noted in an article published in 2000 in the Journal of Roman Archaeology . title: Does written language speed up or slow down cultural change?
summary: The written word has been revolutionary in preserving ideas from the past, and transmitting new ones in the present. But does it favor tradition or change?
body: The written word is one of humanity's most important information technologies. Without it, mathematical and scientific discoveries would be lost to history. But it can also lock ideas in place long after they've stopped making sense. So does writing speed up cultural change or slow it down? Russell Gray , a professor in the Department of Linguistic and Cultural Evolution at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, heads a research project investigating how writing affects the way languages change. His team uses methods borrowed from evolutionary biology to trace languages through family trees — similar to the way biologists trace species. Language is one element of culture that researchers can measure to determine whether writing speeds up or slows down cultural change. "The obvious answer," Gray said, is that writing slows culture down because writing "is all codified and specified and people get trained in it." Gray doesn’t think the obvious answer is necessarily the right one. But other researchers agree that writing can lock in ways of thinking. body: Flu season is off to an early start in some parts of the U.S., data shows. In a typical year, U.S. flu activity starts building in late fall — typically in October or November — and peaks between December and February. This year, flu activity is currently low but rising nationwide: During the week ending Sept. 26, 3.4% of respiratory samples tested by clinical labs were positive for flu, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data . That's about seven times the rate that was seen at the same point last year. About 0.5% of samples tested positive during the week ending Sept. 27, 2025. "This particular year, it appears to be starting early — like right now," Dr. William Schaffner , a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health in Tennessee, told Live Science. Patients at clinics in his area are already testing positive for flu, he said. The early uptick in flu is mostly unfolding in Western states, including Washington, California and Arizona . Your eyes are on the stunning scenery, taking in the vistas along Route 66 or the grandeur of the Rocky Mountains, or you're catching up on messages. Your hands barely touch the wheel, and your foot doesn't push a pedal. Your car communicates with others on the road, so there's no need to brake suddenly or swerve. That's because it knows a vehicle five cars up from you has done so, and all those in between are slowing at exactly the right pace to avoid dramatic changes in trajectory. And when you park for the night, your car makes you money, selling the excess energy it's harvested from its paint back to the grid. title: Scientists have identified a 'protein signature' in blood that could predict healthy aging
summary: Having a certain ratio of proteins produced by immune cells in your blood is linked to a higher risk of age-related diseases, scientists report.
body: Two people born on the exact same day can age in totally different ways ‪—‬ one in relative health and the other with chronic disease. Now, scientists have found a key difference in the immune systems of people who are more prone to age-related conditions, and it could help explain why some people remain healthier longer. In young people, the immune system contains many naive T cells , a type of white blood cell. Over time, exposure to pathogens and vaccinations transforms some of these T cells into memory cells , which can respond quickly to defend the body against germs. These memory cells make different types of characteristic proteins, called granzymes, which kill infected cells. They come in different "flavors," including granzyme K and granzyme B. In a new study, published Friday (Oct. 9) in the journal Immunity , scientists found that individuals with more memory cells that make granzyme K than cells that make granzyme B tend to have healthier aging. title: Cool chemistry trick allows new tattoos to 'turn on and off'

Researchers have developed a new type of tattoo ink that can be switched on and off with light, allowing colors and images embedded in the skin to be changed and even "erased" without having to go through the painful tattoo-removal process . The system, which is being commercialized under the name PhotoTat, could eventually give people a way to conceal or change permanent body art. It could also have more practical applications, including medical tattoos that are visible only when a doctor needs to see them, researchers reported in a study published Friday (Oct. 9) in the journal Matter & Light . title: South Korean 'robot dog' became first to run a marathon on a single battery charge — now we know how
summary: A quadruped robot scampered more than 26.2 miles of uneven, hilly terrain alongside human runners without needing to be recharged.
body: A four-legged robot completed a full marathon on a single battery charge, covering 26.2 miles (42.2 kilometers) on a hilly public-road course in South Korea two years ago. Now we know a lot more about how it achieved this record-breaking feat. The dog-like robot, called RAIBO2, finished the 22nd annual Sangju Dried-Persimmon Marathon in just over 4 hours, 19 minutes. The bot's developers say it's the first quadruped robot to have completed an official marathon-distance event without stopping to recharge. They're commonly referred to as "robot dogs" because the movement of their joints in both front and hind legs resembles that of canines. The scientists outlined their findings about the robot's feat, which it achieved Nov. 17, 2024, in a study published Sept. 23 in the journal Nature . This achievement represented a new milestone in overcoming a critical limitation for quadruped robots: endurance.
